claim: All findings rest on two separate samples: a behaviour-only study of 40 participants and an fMRI study of 44 participants, analysed separately rather than pooled.
evidence: Forty healthy participants (14 male, mean age 26.1, range 22–31) participated in Study 1 (behaviour only study), and 44 healthy participants (19 male, mean (SD) age = 30.6 (6.5), range 23–50) participated in Study 2 (fMRI study).
notes: Study 2 is described throughout as a separate estimation ('This model was estimated for Studies 1 and 2 separately'), so any claim of replication is a between-sample consistency claim, not a pooled test. Scopes essentially every empirical claim in the paper.

claim: The fMRI sample size was fixed in advance by a power analysis anchored to the Study 1 effect size, not by data-dependent stopping.
evidence: The number of participants recruited in Study 2 corresponds to the sample size estimated using G*Power 3.1 software ( Faul et al., 2007 ) for a two-way  t -test assessing the difference between two means (matched pairs) based on the results of Study 1 (Cohen’s  d  = 0.56), with alpha error = 0.05 and power (1 − beta) = 0.95, the required sample size was 44.
notes: Load-bearing assumption: the power calculation targets the Solo-vs-Social risk-attitude contrast from Study 1, so it does not license power claims about the fMRI interaction effects that the paper's imaging analyses rest on.

claim: Four of the 44 fMRI participants were dropped from the imaging analysis for head motion, so behavioural and imaging analyses in Study 2 do not run on identical samples.
evidence: The fMRI data from four participants in Study 2 were excluded from the fMRI data analysis because of excessive head motion (>3 mm or >3°).
notes: The methods do not state whether these four were retained in the Study 2 behavioural and happiness-model fits; the exclusion is scoped explicitly to 'the fMRI data analysis'.

claim: The partner's choices were not made by a free agent but generated by a deterministic expected-value-maximising algorithm.
evidence: In order to ascertain constant decisions by the partner, the partner’s decisions were simulated using a simple algorithm that always selected the option with the highest expected value; i.e., it selected the lottery if EV diff >0;  EVdiff  = ( high lottery outcome + low lottery outcome )/2 –  safe outcome .
notes: Single-source contribution: this is invisible from results prose or captions. Any interpretation of the Partner condition as 'someone else chose for me' rests on a belief manipulation whose success the methods do not report checking. It also means partner choice is a deterministic function of EVdiff, so partner_pRPE is not independent of trial parameters.

claim: In the fMRI study the social partner was one of two authors rather than a naive peer, unlike in the behavioural study where partners were paired participants.
evidence: In Study 2, instead of playing against another same-sex participant, participants played either against experimenter MG or TW depending on sex (participant and partner were always of same sex) who were outside the scanner.
notes: Load-bearing for the cross-study replication argument: the social relationship differs between Study 1 and Study 2, so any divergence between studies is confounded with partner identity (peer vs experimenter).

claim: A scripted icebreaker session was run before the task to establish a positive, non-competitive relationship, and post-task partner ratings serve as the manipulation check on that social context.
evidence: Results of a brief questionnaire indicate that this approach was successful: participants’ average ratings of their partners in terms of sympathy, cooperativity, honesty, openness and sociability were all above 8 on a scale of 1–10, in both studies ( Appendix 1—table 11 ).
notes: This is a control/manipulation-check result stated in the methods rather than the results prose. The ratings are ceiling-range with no comparison condition, so they establish that the partner was liked, not that liking caused the effects.

claim: The lottery was resolved independently for participant and partner, so outcome inequality and partner prediction error are dissociable by design rather than by post hoc modelling.
evidence: Importantly, when the risky option was selected in the  Social  or  Partner  condition, the lottery was played out independently for the participant and the partner, such that both could receive the higher ( HighOutcome ) or lower outcome ( LowOutcome ), independently from each other.
notes: This design feature is what makes the guilt/envy and responsibility regressors separable; it bounds the claim that responsibility effects are distinguishable from simple inequality aversion.

claim: Momentary happiness was sampled only on every second trial and Z-scored within participant, so the happiness models fit relative within-subject fluctuation at half the trial resolution, not absolute well-being.
evidence: Every two trials, one ISI after the outcome of the previous trial, participants were asked ‘How happy are you right now?’. ... For analysis, happiness ratings were  Z -scored to cancel out effects of different rating variabilities across participants.
notes: Z-scoring removes between-subject level differences by construction, so no claim about who is happier overall can be supported. It also motivates the omission of the model intercept: 'No constant term was used as ratings were  Z -scored'.

claim: Risk attitude is estimated by two independent routes — a model-free risk premium from a logistic fit and a CARA exponential-utility parameter fitted by probit regression — applied separately to Solo and Social conditions.
evidence: The  risk premium  for each condition was defined as the EVdiff value corresponding to 50%  risky  choices indicated by the fitted logistic regression model. ... Following an econometric method ( von Gaudecker et al., 2011 ), we estimated  ⍴  by fitting a probit regression with a cumulative Gaussian link function  Φ  to choices obtained in the  Solo  and  Social  conditions of each participant
notes: The CARA form is an assumption, not a fitted choice: constant absolute risk aversion imposes no wealth dependence. The two estimators are not independent evidence — both are fits to the same choice data — so convergence between them is a robustness check, not replication.

claim: Five nested happiness models are compared, and the family is constructed so that responsibility-based accounts are tested against inequality-based accounts inherited from prior work.
evidence: We ran five models: (1) a ‘Basic’ model ( Equation 4 ; the winning model in  Rutledge et al., 2014  in which there was no  Social  condition) ... (5) a ‘Responsibility Redux’ model identical to the precedent except for the absence of  partner_pRPE s, as we realized that this regressor explained little variance ( Equation 8 ).
notes: Flag: the fifth model is explicitly data-derived — it was constructed after observing that partner_pRPE explained little variance in these data. Its comparative fit statistics are therefore not an out-of-sample test. The Basic, Inequality and Guilt-envy models are pre-specified ('identical to those used in  Rutledge et al., 2016 ').

claim: Model selection among the happiness models rests on within-sample fit indices and pairwise likelihood ratio tests, with no cross-validation or held-out data.
evidence: To formally assess which of our models fitted the data best, we supplemented the AIC, BIC,  R 2  and adjusted  R 2  values reported in  Table 1  with a series of  likelihood ratio tests : we compared pair-wise the likelihoods of the  Responsibility  model given the data to the likelihoods of all the other models.
notes: The Responsibility model is the fixed reference in every pairwise comparison, i.e. the comparison structure presupposes the favoured model. Likelihood ratio tests are only valid for nested pairs; the methods do not state that all five are nested (the Inequality and Guilt-envy models are not nested within Responsibility).

claim: Parameter recovery on noise-added synthetic data establishes that the happiness-model parameters are identifiable.
evidence: After fitting each participant’s momentary happiness data (see above), we synthesized new momentary happiness data based on each participant’s estimated parameters, added 1SD of noise to the happiness data, fitted the model to these synthetic data, and repeated this procedure 10 times, for both studies. ... The results show that the estimated parameters could be reliably recovered from noisy synthetic data.
notes: This is a control result asserted in the methods, so it is extractable from my slice, but the quantitative support lives in Figure 3—figure supplement 1, which I do not see. Recovery is demonstrated only for the generating model — it does not address model identifiability (whether Responsibility and Guilt-envy can be told apart from data).

claim: The BOLD analysis of computational variables uses regressors whose amplitudes come from the happiness model already fitted to the same participants' ratings.
evidence: Those regressors were applied as follows to each experimental session of each participant: (1) fitting the computational model to the momentary happiness data; (2) creation of a series of stick functions representing the time of occurrence of the modelled events during the scan, with stick magnitude determined by the fitted value calculated by the model; and (3) convolution of the series of stick functions with the canonical BOLD function (as implemented in SPM).
notes: Load-bearing assumption: neural correlates of social_pRPE are correlates of a quantity defined by the winning happiness model. If that model is misspecified, the imaging result inherits the misspecification. The methods describe only how these regressors were built — they state no result about which regions responded.

claim: The connectivity analyses seed from clusters defined by group-level contrasts in the same dataset, with a single fixed seed applied to every participant.
evidence: We ran two models for each participant, both based on GLM1, with the following seeds: the left insula cluster more sensitive to the outcomes of  Risky  vs . Safe  choices, yielding GLM3 (see  Figure 4D, E ), and the left STS cluster responding more to  social_pRPE  than  partner_pRPE , yielding GLM4 ( Figure 4H ). Seeds were identical for all participants.
notes: Flag non-independence: seeds are selected by the very contrasts whose effects the paper interprets, so the seed regions are not independently defined. Fixed seeds also assume anatomical correspondence across participants after normalisation.

claim: The ROI mixed-model analyses of BOLD treat individual voxels as observations with subject as the only random factor, giving observation counts in the tens to hundreds of thousands.
evidence: Similar to the behavioural data, we analysed GLM1 parameter estimates from voxels of specific regions of interest (see Results) using mixed-effects linear regressions with residual ε ij  ∼  N (0,  σε 2 ) and subject-specific random effects  uj  ∼  N (0,  σu 2 ). ... In all models,  Subject  was the only random factor (random intercept).
notes: Auditor flag, single-source: voxels within an ROI are spatially smoothed (8 mm FWHM) and therefore strongly dependent, so N values reported in Appendix 1—tables 4–10 (e.g. N = 947,840 for dmPFC) are not independent observations. The resulting p-values and standard errors are anticonservative; effect directions are interpretable but significance levels from these models should not be read as participant-level inference. Corrected whole-brain SPM results are not affected by this.

claim: Scanning run is a significant factor in several ROI models, meaning some reported BOLD effects are not stable across the two sessions, and this instability is left undiscussed.
evidence: We note here that the  Run  factor and interactions with it had significant effects in several ROIs, which shows that some of the effects reported varied across runs. However, for the sake of brevity, we will not discuss these results further.
notes: Single-source contribution: this qualification appears only in the appendix table legends and bounds the generality of the ROI effects. The authors themselves state the effects varied across runs; the paper's main-text claims are presumably run-collapsed.

claim: Whole-brain imaging inference is thresholded at cluster-level FWE p < 0.05 with a cluster-forming threshold of p < 0.001 uncorrected, with small-volume correction used only where stated.
evidence: All clusters reported survive a significance threshold of p < 0.05 with family-wise error correction for multiple comparisons across the whole brain or a smaller volume when explicitly mentioned, based on an uncorrected voxel-wise (cluster-forming) threshold of  p  < 0.001.
notes: The disjunction 'whole brain or a smaller volume' means the correction volume must be checked per cluster; the methods do not state which contrasts used small-volume correction or how those volumes were defined.

claim: Everything measured is choice behaviour, self-reported happiness, and BOLD correlation; no variable is experimentally manipulated except who made the decision and for whom.
evidence: There were three kinds of trials: decisions by the participant only for themselves ( Solo  condition), decisions by the participant for themselves and the partner ( Social  condition), and decisions by the partner for both themselves and the participant ( Partner  condition).
notes: Inference across the methods as a whole rather than a single quoted sentence, hence tentative. The condition manipulation is genuine and within-subject, but all neural and model-parameter findings are correlational: no intervention on brain activity or on responsibility per se. If the paper's framing states that responsibility or a brain region causes happiness changes, the methods support only a conditional association.

claim: Stakes are small monetary amounts in the range of tens of cents, played out per trial.
evidence: Gain amounts were selected randomly out of the following: [15, 25, 40, 55, 75] cents.
notes: Bounds generalisation of both risk-attitude and guilt/responsibility claims: the CARA parameter and the inequality regressors are estimated over a narrow, low-magnitude payoff range, and constant absolute risk aversion is assumed over that range.
